For those genuinely looking for their baby's name to stand out, you might want to try something stunning and standalone like Elspeth or Mamie. If those tickle your fancy, keep reading for a compilation of names with an unusual quality that's elegant, edgy, and will surely stand the test of time.

Agatha is a very unique option for little girls these days, but it wasn’t always! It stayed in the top 1000 baby names from 1900 to 1945, and hasn’t been seen since. The name Agatha means “good” or “honorable,” which is such a powerful meaning for your little one.

Although it peaked in the nation’s top 100 names in 1880, Agnes fell off the charts sometime in the ‘70s. But the Greek name, which means “pure,” is poised for a comeback. The nickname Aggie, in particular,” has loads of retro charm.

From the 1880s until around the early 1930s, Alma held tight in the top 100 names for girls in the United States. It dropped pretty dramatically in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s and has settled just inside of the top 1000. A name with origins in many cultures, it means “nourishing” or “soul.”

This elegant name started strong in the 1800s, tapered off, shot to its peak in the late 1960s, and has gradually waned in popularity since. Of British and French origin, it means “noble strength.”

Latin for “venerable” or “majestic,” Augusta is grand in all the right ways. It has big great-aunt-who’s-traveled-the-world energy. Huge selling point: Gussie is an unbearably cute nickname.

Barbara is a classic in every sense of the word, and it definitely has an old-fashioned feel. The name Barbara means “foreign” or “strange,” and was most popular from the ‘20s through the ‘60s. You can use Barbie, Babs, or Barb as a cute nickname, too.

Bernie is the absolute cutest girl nickname, and the name Bernadette really sells it. This old-fashioned choice means “brave bear” or “strong,” and it was most popular in the 1920s.

An oldie but a goodie of a Greek name, Beryl means “light green semiprecious gemstone” and is perfect for the baby girl who’s the jewel of your eye.

A feminine name of Hebrew origin, Beulah means “bride.” That might make you think of how fast your daughter will grow up, but look at it like this — that’s a long way off, and it’s something to look forward to when it eventually arrives. Although this name was ranked #123 for girls in the U.S. in 1880, it’s dropped to the #6000-ish range today.

You’d think this name would have seen a bigger resurgence recently with so much love for The Golden Girls! But Blanche, a French name meaning “white” or “pure,” currently sits at #11,298 in popularity for U.S. girl names. For context, it was a top 100 name in the 1880s.

Never a wildly common name, Cicely hovered around the #5,000 mark through most of the early 1900s before dropping to its current ranking of #11,351 for girls. It means “blind of self-beauty.”

The feminine version of Claude, the name Claudette means “lame,” which isn’t all that great — but at least it’s French! It also hasn’t been popular since 1973, so you know she’ll be the only one in her preschool class.

Although Cordelia fell out of favor a little in the late ‘90s, it’s been slowly creeping back up the charts. And why not? This lovely name of Latin origin has the sweetest meaning: “heart.”

This lovely name means “steadfast,” which is exactly what you want your kid to be (except maybe at bedtime!). It feels a little prim, sure, but you could also soften it up by calling her Connie.

This beautiful name is an elaborate form of Cora. It means “little heart,” which perfectly describes your little one. It’s also forever tied to Coretta Scott King, the civil rights leader who carried her husband’s legacy forward for decades.

While the name has had some recent traction thanks to Selling Sunset’s Davina Potratz, it’s a fairly uncommon sweet name that means “beloved” — a sweet nod to your beloved bundle of joy.

From the Greek word delphís, this beautiful baby name means “dolphin” — and how cute is that? The name is also derived from Delphi, the home of an oracle in Greek mythology. It currently ranks #3643 for girl names in the U.S.

Oh goodness, imagine a sweet little baby named Dorothea! It’s just too much. This moniker means “gift of God” and has Greek origins. You can choose nicknames like Thea or Dottie, too, and hasn’t been on the popular chart since 1970.

It’s surprising that this name ranks all the way down at #15927 on the list because it’s really freaking cute! Meaning “sweet, candy,” Dulcie is related to Dulce — the name that inspired Cervantes’ Dulcinea, Don Quixote’s chosen lady.

Want your baby girl to stand strong in her voice? Consider this name, which means “well-spoken” (and happens to be the name of the tough and tenacious Effie White from Dreamgirls). Although Effie ranked #63 in the 1880s, it sits at #2120 today.

I love the simplicity of Ellen. It’s so sweet and lovely, and conjures up images of girls being badasses while also being little dollops of joy — sugar and spice and everything nice. Ellen means “torch” or “bright light” and was in the top 100 of baby girl names for literal decades. Now, it sits at #920.

A strong and sturdy name of Hebrew and Scottish origin, Elspeth means “chosen by God.” While it hasn’t made much headway outside of the U.K., it has a childish charm that might be fit for a sweet comeback.

Is Ethel not the absolute sweetest? This name just brings such joy, and its meaning is “noble.” The last time it hit the popularity charts was in the ‘70s, so I think it’s definitely time to bring back this old-fashioned cutie.

This unique name of Greek origin is perfect for your little one as it means “generous gift.” It also stems from Greek mythology, giving off some goddess vibes, too.

Like Effie, this Greek name means “well-spoken,” but it also means “sweetly speaking” — and, well, that just sounds lovely. Eulalia has a soft, earthy appeal, too, as it’s the name of a tall green grass that grows in Eastern Asia.

Faye had a good run of popularity in the ‘30s, but otherwise hasn’t come close to that same acclaim. It’s still unique now, but I suspect that the fantasy book culture has brought Faye — which means “fairy” or “belief” — back into the fold.

Don't underestimate this name that you might associate with your great-aunt! Meaning "strength of a spear," the German moniker feels a bit flinty but has a cute, much softer nickname in Gertie.

This Welsh name means “land nation,” but it has a quaint and sweet sound to it that defies its definition. And of course, there’s the Motown legend Gladys Knight, which makes it even more legendary.

Henri, Etta, Rett — so many sweet nicknames can come from the name Henrietta. It hasn’t been on the popular lists since 1968, and Henrietta also means “home ruler.”

A form of Esther, Hester means “star.” And whatever, no one cares about the Hester Prynne baggage. In fact, that kind of makes this name even cooler. A heroine who refused to be shamed into submission? Heck yeah.

An abbreviated form of Katherine, this sweet name means "pure." Naturally, it's a purr-fect name for cat lovers. It's also been the name of many famous characters, from Kitty Bennet of Pride and Prejudice to Kitty Pryde of X-Men.

In Roman mythology, Lavinia was the wife of Aeneas and the namesake of an ancient city, so this comes with a bit of historical pedigree. It’s lush and lyrical, not fussy at all, and the nickname Vinnie is so unexpectedly perfect for a little girl.

This lilting name of Hebrew and Arabic origin has beautiful (and sort of mysterious) meanings of “dark beauty” and “born at night.” If you grew up obsessed with Anna Sewell’s classic novel Black Beauty, this could be the old-fashioned girl’s name for your little one.

If you love Haunted Mansion, you undoubtedly know Madame Leota. So, while this name is pretty uncommon (#14,360 for girls’ names in the U.S.), it’s beloved in the Disney fan community. Germanic, it means “of the people.”

Loretta means “laurel,” which has such a sweet, country vibe. Retta, Lo, Etta, Rettie — there are so many cute nickname options for this old-fashioned choice. In the 1910s and ‘20s, this name was always in the top 150, and then ended up in the top 100 for pretty much all of the ‘30s.

A lovely name that means “little and womanly,” Lottie is a diminutive of the French name Charlotte. It has a “je ne sais quoi” flair that is due for a comeback... especially with the popular characters of the same name from Disney’s The Princess and the Frog and Showtime’s Yellowjackets.

I just love this one so much — it sounds like a storybook character! The name Louise means “renowned warrior,” which is pretty amazing, and while it’s gaining some traction on the popularity charts, it’s still a unique choice. (It was most popular in the 1910s.)

How sweet is Mabel? The name literally means “lovable,” and while it has gotten more popular in recent years, it’s still a unique choice for your little one. Before 2013, it hadn’t been on the popular charts since 1964.

Thanks to Hilary Duff (or Parenthood fave Mae Whitman), this darling little moniker could make a comeback, but Mae is definitely still considered old-fashioned. It’s often a diminutive of names like Margaret or Mary, but it stands on its own very well. It’s just so spunky and cute. Mae also means “maiden” or “young woman” and was in the top 100 baby girl names from 1900 to 1920.

Maude is just so punchy, I’m obsessed. This cute old-fashioned girl name hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1950, and it means “powerful in battle.” Hell yeah, girl!

This adorable name, a shorter version of Margaret or another form of Mary, was famously chosen by Meryl Streep for her daughter Mamie Gummer. It means “pearl” and “star of the sea,” both beautiful metaphors for your new treasure.

Midge stems from the Greek word for “pearl” — but you may better recognize it as the name of the title character in Prime Video’s hit series The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel. Although the name dropped off in popularity in the ‘70s, it’s making a gradual comeback, currently ranking #2603.

This elegant English name means “gentle strength” and encapsulates both maturity and tenderness, making it a fantastic choice for the well-rounded daughter you want to raise.

Millicent just sounds vintage right off the bat, and its popularity journey truly makes that case — it hasn’t been on the lists since 1965. You can go with Millie for a cute nickname, but I truly do think Millicent just sounds so cool. It also means “strong in work.”

Who can forget Moaning Myrtle from Harry Potter? But this cute name has a richer history than that. Its origins come from the “evergreen shrub,” which was sacred to the goddess Venus as a symbol of love. So, in some ways, this name could symbolize your everlasting love for your baby girl.

OK, this might be what you call your grandmother, but it has a cute ring to it, too. The Hebrew name, which means "grace," has a uniquely modern, feminine vibe that stands out.

This gender-neutral name of Old Norse origins boasts many meanings: “wealth,” “honor,” “respect,” “man’s defender,” and “ancestor’s relic.” So, if you’re pretty sure your kid is destined to be a wild card, Ola it is! This name ranked in the top 200s during the 1880s, but today it has settled in around the #6800 mark.

Patricia feels incredibly traditional, but Patty for a little girl? Come on, we’ve got to bring it back. Patricia means “noble” and is a variant of Patrick if you like the Irish connection.

Doesn’t this just sound like it belongs to the main character of a cozy British mystery? Greek for “beloved,” it boasts a bunch of punchy nicknames like Mena, Pippa, and Pip.

OK, OK, bear with me — Prudence is extremely old-fashioned, but it also has the delightful nickname of Prue! Prudence means “wise,” “skilled,” or “intelligent,” and was extremely common during the Middle Ages. (It hasn’t been in the top 1000 baby girl names since 1948, either.)

Thanks to Dolly Parton’s immense popularity, the name Jolene has shot up the rankings in recent years. But this twangy name, which is a variant of Rae, is a much less common option (#10,919 for girl names in the U.S.) that offers the same spirit.

Calling all Ravenclaws! Harry Potter fans who call this house home will surely recognize Rowena as the first name of its founder. Outside of its HP claim to fame, the name means “famous friend” and “pure spear.” Plus, it comes with the cool nickname Ro.

Oh, Susannah! Don’t you cry for me! Whether you spell it Suzanna, Susanna, or with the traditional H at the end, this name is a classic. Susannah means “lily,” so it has a sweet, nature-related connection and a ton of cute nicknames, from Susie (or Suzie) to Suze and Anna. It was only in the top 1000 of baby girl names from 1967 to 1978, and even then, it was still one of the more unique options.

Thelma was popularized by the 1887 novel by Marie Corelli, and it means “will” in Greek. It’s peak grandma chic! And if you have two daughters, Thelma and Louise is right there. (Kidding... mostly.)

Theodora is the feminine form of Theodore, meaning “gift of God.” It’s just so cute, and Theo is a darling name for a little girl (so is Teddy, honestly!). From 1954 to 2019, it didn’t even top the charts, but it’s making a slow comeback.

Wilhelmina is just so gorgeous, and I love all of the nicknames you can pick for this one. The name also means “resolute protector,” so it feels like a strong moniker for your little gal. Bonus: It hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1952, so you know it’s unique.

This lovely Welsh name means "blessed peace," which, sure, doesn't exactly align with everyone's favorite Winifred — the iconic red-haired witch from Hocus Pocus. But the name has a sophisticated feeling to it, and the nickname Winnie is just so delightful.

This article was originally published on July 2, 2024

Ever wondered if those used coffee grounds could be helping your houseplants? If you’re looking for a few ready-made pick-me-ups, here’s what you can give your indoor plants

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones. Quite often, thanks to social media and online forums, we’ll hear about some novel way to use key scraps to help plants. These quirky DIY tricks can seem so compelling and easy (and also free) that it’s tempting to toss scraps straight into the potting soil around your plants.

A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way. But that last bit is important. You need to make sure you are using the right kind of scraps, and that you have prepared them so they can be absorbed or processed well. Fail to do this, and there’s a chance that helpful impulse could result in fuzzy mold and tiny gnats.

The kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery. These scraps all need prep first, though, whether that's drying, grinding or some time in a compost pile or worm bin. If you want to unlock their gentle benefits, this is a good time to get things moving. Houseplants slow down as the days get shorter, so they don't need much extra food until spring – giving you time to turn some trash into treasure.

When it comes to the best scraps for houseplants, preparation and application are key. Never dump wet, chunky food scraps onto the soil surface, as they can trap stagnant moisture and invite houseplant pests. Instead, use one of these preparation methods: air or oven-drying, grinding into fine powder, brewing, or indoor composting with a worm bin.

Indoor composting bins don’t require lots of knowledge or experience these days, and you can pick up units that make composting a highly beneficial background activity. If you’re interested in a compact unit for indoors, the Original VermiHut System, available from Amazon, is a neat and super-easy way to turn scraps into rich, houseplant-safe worm castings. Once your scrap of choice has been treated, you can gently work small amounts into the top inch (2.5cm) of potting mix.

Prioritize pot hygiene with any scraps you do try out. Check that every container has unobstructed drainage holes and keep a close eye on treated pots for 2-3 weeks. If you spot any white fuzz, scrape it off and allow the top layer to dry. Remember that kitchen scraps are meant to be gentle supplemental boosters, not replacements for quality potting soil and a balanced seasonal feeding routine. Here are 6 scraps you can safely try with your houseplants – plus, which scraps to leave in the bin.

The buzz around coffee grounds for houseplants is mostly about nitrogen (along with trace potassium and magnesium). That nitrogen is tied up in organic matter, though, and soil microbes will need to break it down before the roots can use it. Select plain, unflavored Arabica or Robusta grounds, and avoid flavored coffees containing synthetic oils, syrups, or spices.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Never spread damp grounds thickly over indoor soil, as they can mold and dry into a crust that repels water. Instead, spread used grounds on a baking sheet to dry, then blend a small handful (no more than 5-10% of total volume) into a fresh potting mix, or process through an indoor worm bin first. Contrary to myth, brewed grounds will not reliably acidify your potting soil, as brewing pulls a good share of the acid into your cup. For a good potting mix, buy Espoma Organic Potting Mix from Walmart.

Eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate, and plants need calcium to strengthen cell walls and support healthy new leaf development. But don’t toss large shell fragments into a houseplant pot. Calcium carbonate dissolves at a glacial pace, especially in neutral or alkaline potting mixes. Instead, rinse away the egg white, let shells air-dry for 48 hours, and pulverize them into a fine powder.

For grinding, use a dedicated grinder, a pestle and mortar, or a processor like the Cuisinart Mini Food Processor from Amazon, which is compact and super-fast. For a faster mineral release, soak the shell powder in a splash of mild lemon juice or vinegar for 24 hours. The mild acid reacts with the calcium carbonate to create plant-available calcium citrate. Just remember to dilute before applying. Work a light pinch into potting soil once or twice a year, skipping acid-loving plants like African violets, as the calcium can gradually raise soil pH.

Banana peels (along with closely related plantain peels) are rich in potassium, which regulates water uptake and boosts flowering. They also contain trace phosphorus and magnesium. However, burying chunks of raw banana or plantain peel in your houseplant’s potting soil is a really bad idea. Dense, sugary peels rot sluggishly in pots, attracting fruit flies and encouraging root-rotting pathogens.

Chop banana (or plantain) peels into small pieces and process in a compost bin or worm farm until crumbly, before blending into potting mix. Alternatively, dehydrate clean peels in a low oven until crispy, grind them into a powder, and sprinkle a spoonful into the soil. While soaking peels in water for 48 hours creates a mild banana tea, it leaches only trace nutrients. If you’re looking for targeted liquid feeds, you’re better off with a balanced fertilizer such as Espoma’s Organic Indoor 2-2-2 Plant Food, available from Walmart, and adding it during spring and summer growth.

Plain, steeped tea leaves offer gentle organic matter, trace nitrogen, and mild tannic acids that subtly condition soil structure and improve moisture retention. However, you need to stick to unflavored black, green, white, or pure herbal teas like chamomile or rooibos. And make sure they are steeped without milk, sugar, or honey. Avoid heavily spiced chai blends or artificially flavored teas, as the essential oils can irritate delicate root hairs.

Tear open used tea bags and discard the pouch, as most tea bags contain plastic fibers. Never pile wet leaves on top of the soil, as they can encourage gnats and mold. Instead, spread the loose leaves on a paper towel until dry and lightly fork a teaspoon into the topsoil, or drop them into a worm bin. Used gently once a month in spring and summer, they give moisture-loving tropicals like ferns, calatheas, and pothos a gentle lift. If you don’t have any compost going, Home Depot carries Noble Worm Organics Worm Castings, and a little of that does the same job.

Pungent alliums like onions and garlic, spicy peppers, or fibrous potato skins should never be buried straight into pots. They can ferment and summon fungus gnats. However, you can safely capture minerals by making a liquid tonic from key vegetable scraps. Save the cooled, unsalted water left over from boiling or steaming nutrient-dense vegetables like carrots, potatoes, broccoli, or leafy greens. Use this mineral-rich water at room temperature instead of watering once or twice a month, discarding any leftovers after 24 hours so bacteria cannot multiply.

Alternatively, you can route clean trimmings through an indoor worm bin. Bury solid scraps like carrot peelings, lettuce cores, and squash trimmings beneath damp bedding in a compact indoor worm bin. In 8-12 weeks, red wigglers can convert them into odorless vermicompost. You can buy Uncle Jim’s Worm Farm Live Red Wigglers from Amazon for hardworking composting worms to transform carrot peels and used greens into nutrient-rich castings. Then add to plants, applying 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per quart (0.95 L) of potting mix around the base, and water in.

Rinsing uncooked white, brown, or jasmine rice leaves behind cloudy, starch-rich water containing trace amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) along with B vitamins. While scientific evidence shows its direct fertilizer value is modest and varies widely by grain type, those gentle starches can act as a mild prebiotic snack for beneficial soil microbes in healthy potting mixes. However, use only fresh, unsalted and unseasoned rinse water (or cooled, unsalted boiling water).

Apply it the same day in place of a standard watering once a month. Never store rice water in jars to ferment. DIY fermented rice water quickly breeds foul-smelling bacteria. Likewise, avoid salted pasta water. While plain starchy pasta water is harmless, even a pinch of cooking salt accumulates in closed pots and can quickly reach a level where it scorches roots. If you’re after a good indoor watering can, choose something with a gooseneck spout that can target the base of the plant, such as the Megawodar Copper Watering Can from Amazon.

Even with careful prep, certain kitchen leftovers need to be kept far away from your indoor garden. Meat, fish, and dairy products are the big ones. Oily and greasy foods are also non-starters. Animal proteins and fats rot rapidly in warm indoor temperatures, creating unbearable odors, attracting flies, and coating soil particles in a waterproof film that suffocates roots.

Salty and sugary leftovers are equally destructive. Salted pasta water, soup broths, and seasoned cooking liquids leave behind sodium deposits that build up in closed pots, drawing moisture out of roots and leaving foliage with crispy brown leaf tips. Meanwhile, sugary sauces, fruit juices, and citrus rinds trigger fungal growth and attract household ants.

When monitoring your houseplants in the weeks after adding your kitchen scraps, keep a close eye out for fuzzy molds and fungus gnats. Used early, you can add sticky traps like LightsMax Dual-Sided Yellow Sticky Traps from The Home Depot to manage adult gnats and other flying pests.

By drying, grinding, or brewing, or letting an indoor worm bin do the heavy lifting first, you can enrich your potting mix sustainably and give your houseplants a gentle helping hand with ingredients destined for the trash.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8158. Gary Vaynerchuk Just Wants Us All To Be (And Raise) Nice Guys

“I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”

If you haven’t seen Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere, make a date with Netflix. This is must-see TV for parents, especially parents raising boys. But a word of warning, it’s like a scary movie that will haunt you well after the credits run. Weapons has nothing on the horror show that is the manosphere.

In the documentary, Theroux, the understated British journalism, calmly and a bit coldly explores the manosphere from the inside. In talking to the most extreme influencers — the peddlers in misogyny and anti-semitism, conspiracy and homophobia — he finds himself pulled in to the fight, made into content, taken out of context, and expertly trolled, even as he holds the camera. “He really don’t wanna be in the live,” one such British influencer says to the camera in front of Theroux on a particularly disturbing night out. “He don’t wanna be on the content. But he’s got no choice.”

We parents, on the other hand, do have a choice — to shield our kids from the depravity, to push back against the cultural creep, and to turn to other influencers. Influencers like Gary Vaynerchuk, the best-selling author, radio host, entrepreneur, and an unabashed dude who plays his part as the antidote to the vitriol of the manosphere. As an executive — CEO of VaynerMedia and Chairman of VaynerX — he’s a hard-nosed, fast-talking entrepreneur who believes in bootstrapping life. He also fundamentally believes in kindness. “I know I was well parented,” he tells Fatherly, “and I have all of my validation, and I mean all of it, wrapped up in being a nice guy.”

Parents can choose to be nice, sure, but Vaynerchuk also notes we can choose to be more accountable, to stop coddling our kids on one hand while taking charge on the other (taking away their social media access or phones if we need to). “Supporting your child is everything,” says Vaynerchuk. “Enabling your child is a disaster.” And walking that tightrope between the two? That’s parenting.

The following interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Gary Vaynerchuk is an unapologetically wealthy entrepreneur. But his empasis on self-improvement and kindness poses an important question: What’s the point of being rich if you’re an unhappy jerk?

What do you think is the real reason people are checking out — from the workforce but also social life — and how can we inoculate our kids, and especially boys, against this?

Gary Vaynerchuk: I think modern parenting has lost its way. I think we've made a couple of crucial mistakes, and we're blaming it on social media because we don't like accountability. Mistake number one: I do think, especially for boys, we got a little too into eighth-placed trophies, a little too "fighting isn't the way to resolve things", a little too coddle-y-coddle-y. Listen, I'm a mama's boy through and through. I also got into ten fights in school, and my mom had no opinions about it, meaning it was like, "Yeah, life." I think we've gotten too in our kids' business. Again, everyone grows up in different circumstances. There's plenty of kids right now that don't have parents in their business.

Forget about the '80s and '90s. From the '70s and '60s, '50s and '40s, '30s and '10s, '00s, and on back to the 1800s … parents did not go to school and yell at teachers for giving their kid a B instead of an A. But that is what has happened the last 20 years. ... The f*ck are we texting our sons who are 27 because we have the family f*cking plan and knowing where everyone is? Let men be men.

Who do you think wins in a fight: a lion that grew up in the Bronx Zoo, or a lion in the jungle?

We've raised a lot of zoo lions in the last 25 years. We need to take a little bit of our foot off the pedal.

What role do you think sports play in teaching some of this wildness, some of this conflict?

I think it's everything. When my son was growing up, during a game, if there was a kid that cried when they lost, I used to, with the parents' permission, I would be like, "It's good that you're crying kid. Don't listen to your parents." Multiple parents were happy that I was doing that for their kid.

I think if you have a kid that cries when they lose in sports, you've been given a blessing. And I think you should compound that, not suppress it. Teaching your kids that nothing matters is a bad idea — leads to depression. If someone said to me around a game of monopoly tonight, "Bro, it's just a game." I'd be like, "F*ck you, man. This is life. When I play, I'm playing for life." So I think sports is everything, but I think parents get involved too much yelling at the coach. Let the coach cook — even if the coach sucks.

Let [your kid] deal with a sucky coach, because you're going to have a sucky boss. Dad's going to have a sucky day. You're going to have a sucky governor one day in your life. Get used to people that have authority or leverage over you. You're going to interact with a sucky policeman. You're going to have a sucky doctor. You have f*cking 27-year-old men throwing temper tantrums because they never were taught how to deal with sucky authority.

Talk to me about humility. How do we get more of it?

Sports is where I learned humility, and it is my superpower. My mom would've not raised a humble child. I thought I was Superman. I literally thought I was the most athletic and most handsome person on earth somewhere around fourth grade. Because in my neighborhood, I had the best hand-eye coordination. And in my neighborhood, I was a little bit better athletically … I won a lot, and then it started to change. And that was a rude awakening. I mean, going through the journey of humility, first getting used to the taste.

I would lose, play again. I would lose, play again. I annoyed people. I feel it's now coming clear to me, literally in real time right now with you, I feel like in second, third, fourth grade, I might've had excuses. So it took some time to acquire that taste, but much like caviar, much like sweetbreads and truffles … oysters, that initial [taste] is like, "Oh, it's a little weird."

And now I love the acquired taste. [Similarly] I now love humility. I love it. It got me here. And now that I'm, quote-unquote, "at some level of success", and I know people look at me, I love that the kids see my humility in meetings behind the scenes. I hope it inspires them to realize it's a beautiful trait, not a loser trait.

You recognize losing is learning. There's a sweetness to that.

Brother, I'm a little bit even weirder. I like losing. I swear to God, I like it, man. I like adversity. I like it. I'm addicted to the underdog, when someone's an underdog, and then they become the champ. Or the reverse; Kobe, Tiger Woods. Tiger, early, loved, loved [them] early. But then I was like, when he was the main guy, I was like, "Ah."

I’d like to jump into something you've said before and my wife and I use it a lot: "Your kid is not your friend." I have a teen right now. I think that truth has kind of hit me hard fairly recently. Do you still believe that, and why? What's the motivation behind it? What's the evidence?

I mean, the evidence is I'm 50 fucking years old and I get 10,000 DMs a day, and I read the content, and I analyze the content. If you're not the person for your child that teaches consequences and ramifications, it's going to be a problem. They'll learn it. Life will teach them, starting at 22, which ... F*ck, man, to unlearn 22 years of that behavior ...

Listen, supporting your child is everything. Enabling your child is a disaster, and that is a fine f*cking line. It's been amazing in so many ways to watch the generation of women that are [now] 48-years-old and are straight best friends with their 15-year-old daughter. Kids are older, and parents are younger, so it makes sense to me. I think it's actually beautiful, but I think there's a lot of moms who lose the plot in the beauty of ... the nirvana of such a gorgeous relationship, and I think they feel the ramifications later, and they need to be eyes wide open.

Being friendly is amazing. You know [parents tell me], "No, Gary, you don't get it. I want them to come to me. I couldn't go to my mom." Yeah, your mom was treating you inappropriately too far in the other direction, but they come to you because you're their f*cking drug dealer. You're dealing the drug of non-accountability. You're dealing the drug of no consequences. You're giving them a little hit of, "It's everyone else's fault but yours."

I'm wondering how that practically plays out when it comes to money. How do you teach your kids about money, the hustle, the passion, work?

Very easy. You stop giving it to them. And the question becomes, when? I have a big thing of 15, 16, 17, 18 feels in the right range. My parents make fun of me on this. If they watch this, they'll call me and be like, "Eh, eight, nine, seven, 10." They were earlier. But, man, I will say, and this is tough, because I know a lot of dads are going to hear this, if you have a 23-year-old son who you're giving money to, you are destroying that child. They have to stand on their own two feet financially. Look, the old days, AKA the '80s and '90s, kids did borrow money from parents to get their first home, but they paid them back … with interest. That's a foreign concept.

Let me just drop the atomic bomb on everyone that I unearthed eight years ago. I started getting these weird DMs and messages from guys who were 25 sh*tting on their parents for giving them money. I didn't understand, brother. I really didn't. I have the humility to say that the first couple times I read stuff that was similar to this, it just wasn't on my radar yet.

Let me get you all to the punchline: If you have a 27-year-old right now that you're giving money to, he's saying all the right things to you in your face, but let me tell you what he's thinking at 11:00 at night when he takes his second Tito's on the rocks: he thinks that you think he's a loser.

He's taking it because he wants to keep up with the Joneses. He wants to be able to take his girl on a date. He wants to go on vacation. He wants to get a nice TV in his pad. He wants to have an Equinox membership. He wants to have Uber. He wants to have Starbucks. But I'm telling you, through your actions, are saying to him that you don't respect him as a man.

Because he's not independent of you. The focus should be on independence, right?

I don't think this is red-pilled or anything. A man at 27 should be providing for, minimally, himself, however humble he lives. I lived in a sh*tty apartments with four friends in college because I used my money, even in college.

And it helps us for peace of mind, not financial success. I'm aware that I'm a public businessman, but when I talk about success and winning, I talk about peace of mind, lack of anxiety, not being in depressive moments. I don't know if you not paying for your kid is going to make them financially successful. I do know it's going to make them a man. I just did another podcast earlier. I'm doing a bunch today. Someone said, "Who do you admire?" I said, "Somebody that works two jobs and takes care of their family, and doesn't complain."

I admire a man or a woman that provides for their family financially on backbreaking effort without a peep of complaining. Boy, do I put that person on a pedestal. And you add nice? Nice? That’s ultimate.

#8157. 13 Easy Holiday Mocktail Recipes For Entertaining Guests (Or Just Yourself)

Sometimes you just need a special bevvie.

I love a good drink — whether it’s a canned cocktail or a jam jargarita, sign me up. But even I sometimes fall back on a good old mocktail, whether I just can’t handle a red wine hangover tomorrow or because I’m hosting and there needs to be an NA option. These easy holiday mocktail recipes are perfect for those moments when you need to whip up a big batch of something festive to drink that’s safe for the whole family. Some are nonalcoholic versions of cocktails you know and love, while others are just fun, festive drinks to serve in place of something spiked.

Since they make nonalcoholic and boozy ginger beer, ginger beer-based recipes are some of the easiest to make into mocktails on the fly. All The Healthy Things’ bevvie is bubbly, fruity, and slightly herby — and it looks so stinking cute with “frosted” cranberries on top.

I love it when a mocktail recipe makes up for its lack of booze with an overabundance of fun in another form. In Averie Cooks’ recipe for caramel apple cider, it’s a homemade caramel sauce all around the rim — I’m in. You could totally use store-bought sauce to save time, but if you have to simmer the cider anyway, it might be fun to try.

If you’re making drinks for guests who don’t mind something super sweet (kids will lose it for this stuff), you’ve got to make Princess Pinky Girl’s Grinch punch. It’s a bright green blend of sherbet, green Hawaiian Punch, Sprite, and juice, so it will hurt many people’s teeth. But sweet-toothed friends, this one’s for you.

Holiday party snuck up on you and you’re in charge of drinks? Whip up this super easy holiday punch from Damn Delicious. All you have to do is mix together some ginger ale, pineapple juice, and cranberry juice, and load it up with some fresh fruits before serving.

Want a more decadent drink for a movie marathon at home? You have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s apple cider float recipe. It’s basically like a milkshake and apple cider had a baby and then dressed it up in warm, seasonal spices.

Think about how happy you’d be if you showed up at a holiday party and there was a self-serve vat of hot chocolate waiting for you. Well, be the change you wish to see in the world with Princess Pinky Girl’s Crockpot peppermint hot chocolate. While technically not a mocktail in that it’s not imitating a cocktail, a gussied-up take on hot chocolate still feels really festive and exciting to try.

This apple cider shrub mocktail from Budget Bytes is the drink if you like a not-so-sweet mocktail that tastes almost like it could be boozy. The drink has a few steps that’ll make you look like a professional bartender, but it’s easy enough that even a first-timer around a cocktail shaker can pull it off. Bonus points: They’re also incredibly cheap to make.

Dirty soda, as a drink category, got plenty of attention this year thanks to the cast of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. So if you need a fun NA drink to serve your reality TV-loving friends, what could be better? Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe will teach you how to get the perfect balance of flavors if it’s your first time wading into dirty soda territory.

Haute & Healthy Living’s pomegranate sparkler looks like the perfect thing to swirl around in one hand while you make a cozy dinner. It still feels special — when else do most of us spring for pomegranate juice? — and has seasonal touches that give you all the festive feels of a cocktail.

Our Love Language Is Food’s spiced cider mocktail proves that as long as you have a fancy glass and a sugar-and-spice rim, you can make your beverage feel celebratory. These just look aggressively clink-able.

Want to make a big batch of punch for the party? Haute & Healthy Living’s recipe blends apple juice, orange concentrate, and cranberry cocktail, plus a few extra touches to bring it to life. It’s so easy to make, you can refill the bowl in a few minutes mid-party.

If you just can’t with all the sweet this and spiced that, Simply LaKita’s blackberry thyme mocktail is perfect for you. It’s simple, fizzy, and way less dessert-in-a-glass-inspired that many winter mocktails tend to be.

Which mocktails are you adding to your hosting repertoire this year?

#8155. “Do I Have To Go To College?”

The author of 'Go The F*ck to College' explores the pride and pain of sending your kid out into the world on their own, once and for all.

For parents of sleepless young ones, the celebrity of Adam Mansbach is hard to overstate. Bleary-eyed and maybe a little despairing, that first time a parent picks up his tome Go the F*ck to Sleep can be a little transcendent. The irreverent picture book perfectly captures the complex feelings we all experience with toddlers — of being trapped in an exhausting simmering pot of cuddles and dependence and sweetness and frustration. Mansbach let it boil over and we parents found a cathartic laugh. 15 years later, Mansbach is tapping once again into the impossible feelings of parents who are about to send off their children — now teens — to the world, to college. Go the F*ck to College, which is available now everywhere you gets books, is just as sweet, sardonic, and endearingly cathartic as Go the F*ck to Sleep. Even for those of us with pre-teens, it’s a wonderful reminder that the parenting journey is long and fraught, difficult and beautiful — and that it would do use good to find a little humor in it. Here, Adam Mansbach reflects, with fewer curse words and no pictures, on the swirling state he finds himself in as he grapples with just how ready his child is to embark on their own into the world. - Tyghe Trimble, Fatherly

My heart rate soared as I typed an answer: I mean, we already bought the sweatshirts. (Those sweatshirts say Bard College – their dream school, to which they'd been accepted months earlier. We bought like twelve of them.)

But you know I'm in favor of a gap year, I added. What are you thinking?

I just want to live at home. I could be a barista.

Fine with me, I said, trying to play it cool.

Market's kind of saturated, I replied. You'd be better off selling tomatoes.

Thank you for being so supportive, Vivien wrote back. That was heartwarming. Ur f*cking lying, bro.

The thing is, I wasn't lying. I wish I had been, but my excitement, my racing heart, my fake nonchalance — they were all because my true (and truly embarrassing) reaction was Yesssssss! They're not leaving! Everything can stay the same forever! In that moment, I was perfectly willing to trade the exultation I felt when I thought about all the ways Vivien's world was about to get beautifully big for the safe, the familiar, and unlimited free lattes.

It was a good reminder that parenting is all about embracing paradox. If you can't hold opposite ideas in your mind, you might go insane.

When your kids are small, the paradoxes are simple – being consumed with blinding rage when their refusal to go to sleep leaves you trapped in a two-hour snuggle with the person you love most, for example, as I wrote about in a little book called Go the F*ck to Sleep.

A decade later, the paradox might be wrapping your head around the fact that a twelve-year-old is sometimes eighteen and sometimes six – or, as a friend of mine summarized the middle school parenting experience, f*ck you, tuck me in. By high school, it's the realization that the only thing more infuriating than seeing your kid lost in their phone is texting them and not getting a reply within four nanoseconds.

And as the clock ticks down on graduation, adulthood, independence, the paradoxes grow thornier. For me — beyond the interplay of exultation and melancholy that turned an April Fools joke inside out, or the complexity of letting my kid know they can always come home while also informing them that I'm turning their bedroom into a gym — the biggest paradox is wanting to do the most parenting when the least is needed.

The moment I realized I could no longer solve all Vivien's problems stands out vividly in my mind. It was fourth grade, and their favorite teacher had announced that she was leaving the school. Vivien felt betrayed and crushed — and because I was powerless to affect the situation, I did something I find far more difficult: sat and listened and went through it with them. However, because I am solution-oriented, or a knucklehead, or because I hate to see my kids in pain, the lesson didn't stick. And so year after year, I've erred on the side of saying here's what you need to do instead of that sounds hard and I'm sure you'll figure it out.

Eventually, I got a little better at it. And Vivien turned out capable and resourceful anyway — not least because I taught them to stand up to overbearing authority figures, by which I mean me. But now, with college looming, I find myself scrambling to impart all the wisdom I've grown wise enough to shut up and keep to myself. The problem is, it's either stuff they already know ("No pills, no powders"), precious nuggets that reveal themselves as idiotic the second I say them out loud ("take classes about things you think are interesting!") or jewels whose importance are rivaled only by the impossibility of trying to turn them into prescriptive advice ("learn to quickly discern who is a trustworthy friend who will push you to be the best version of yourself and who is drawn to you because they're an emotional vampire and you're an emotional blood source!")

So as tempted as I am, I'm not giving my kid a last-minute crash course in everything before I drop them off at college. These final months are no time to establish a new exercise routine or learn basic auto maintenance; they're about enjoying each other's company and purchasing copious bedding. College is the crash course in everything, and nobody's a finished product — not Vivien at eighteen, not me at forty-nine. And maybe the paradox that matters most is that your kid is still your kid even when they're on their own. Or perhaps it's that we grow from the inside out; more than anything, I want Vivien to hold tight to their kidness — the wonder, the silliness, the simple but beautiful moral code they learned in preschool — as they take those first steps into adulthood.

Besides, somebody else at Bard will probably know how to change a tire.

#8152. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Tired of the practically impossible task of packing up the family for a holiday? Here are the best packing cubes for busy families on the go.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

Unleash your little one's love for Lightning McQueen with these top-rated Cars playsets and figures.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!)

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Traveling with kids doesn't;t have to mean getting rid of your entire beauty routine.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Could your child use a little encouragement to read? Disney is here to help with these fabulous books for kids ages 5 to 9.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

Backyard birds tapping on windows is a sometimes funny, sometimes infuriating part of fall. Here's why they do it, and how to stop the behaviour if needs be.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile. Now research and observations from bird experts have revealed the real reasons behind this bizarre behaviour, and you may be surprised to learn what they are.

Some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one. Avian experts, however, have put forward reasons based on cold, hard data, and they provide a fascinating insight into fall bird behaviour.

Whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall. Understanding the likely causes will also help you decide if should take action to stop the window tapping to save birds from harm, and save your sanity, too.

As temperatures decrease in fall, insects become more scarce, many birds are forced to forage for food in new areas. Because glass retains heat from the sun as well as windows allowing some of a home’s heat to escape, any tiny gaps in frames become welcoming nooks for insects to enter diapause (similar to hibernation) – and consequently, one of those spots hungry birds may favor. You might think modern windows don’t offer much space for critters to hole up in, but those drainage weep holes and sliding tracks provide plenty of opportunities. Spiders also use window corners to spin insect-catching webs and lay eggs, offering further protein-rich food to the bird buffet.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO), there’s a rise in birds pecking at windows for food in fall and winter, and in particular by the tit family which includes chickadees and titmice. The organisation also cites that birds may pick at traditional window putty as it’s made with fish or linseed oil, both a valuable source of energy in colder months.

Research carried out by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology found that the lower angle of sunlight hitting windows in fall significantly increases how reflective the glass is. Aside from birds having no concept of what a window is, our feathered friends see differently to us. Most birds have eyes on the sides of their heads to give them almost-360° vision, and while that’s highly useful for spotting potential predators, it means their forward vision isn’t as good as ours. So, reflections in windows are easily interpreted as extra habitat and when birds encounter the glass – which in fall, especially, can appear to them as an invisible barrier – they may peck at it repeatedly to investigate.

Fall is when juvenile birds disperse, and these inexperienced youngsters have a lot to learn about the world around them, and much spatial awareness still to develop. Data published by the American Bird Conservancy and the US Fish & Wildlife Service shows a strong rise in what they term ‘glass interactions’ in fall. While many of these will be window collisions caused by mirror-like glass and navigational error, some will be window pecking led by curiosity as birds investigate their surroundings.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While territorial behaviour among most of our feathered friends peaks in spring, many resident birds claim their territory in fall, according to the National Audubon Society. Northern cardinals, non-migrating American robins, northern mockingbirds, towhees and bluebirds are all highly territorial through fall into winter. And there's a very good reason for this, because as summer broods disperse, thousands of juvenile birds search a new territory. In the face of this competition, existing populations fiercely defend their established territories – especially if it contains a valuable food source such as a garden shrub hung with berries birds love through winter!

With windows becoming mirror-like in the low fall sun, dominant birds can attack their own reflection, mistaking it for a competitor. So this is a common reason why birds tap windows in fall as well as spring.

Whether you have a towhee aggressively pecking at your patio doors or a chickadee tap-tapping your bedroom window at all hours, now you understand what’s behind this behaviour, you can do something about it. Gentle pecking for food harms neither bird nor human, so it’s safe to ignore this low-level behaviour. But more insistent pecking at a window, fighting imagined aggressors or attempting to break through an invisible barrier is not just highly annoying to us but harmful to birds, damaging beaks and wasting valuable energy.

Taking action to stop birds pecking windows involves making glass more visible, or keeping birds away from it in the first place. That means these solutions will also reduce the risk of feathered friends flying into windows and injuring themselves. By working out the likely reason behind a bird tapping on your window, you can choose the method that will be most effective.

Your first step to stop birds tapping windows is to move any houseplants away from windows that are being targeted. To a young bird, a windowsill full of greenery can look like inviting habitat or contribute to the illusion that this could be a continuation of their flightpath.

A quick and cheap solution if the targeted window opens is to shut a length of double-sided reflective bird scare tape like this from Amazon in it. When the tape blows in the wind, its holographic surface casts erratic patterns of ultraviolet light which most birds perceive as a threat. For resident birds in search of tasty insects, this may be enough for them to deem that window an unsafe zone.

While the go-to for making windows more visible to birds and preventing collisions is decals, they're only effective if the gaps between them are narrow enough. A few decals dotted about on a large window are next to useless as birds will likely perceive the areas between them as possible flightpaths, just as they do the gaps between branches in woodland.

A far simpler, more effective and still-stylish alternative is to create a grid of dots around 2 inches apart across the entire window. Use a white oil-based permanent marker like a Sharpie Medium Point Paint Marker, available from Amazon, and for a professional result, use a stencil template. You could make your own by punching holes in cardboard or save yourself the trouble with an Avi-Dot Bird Saver Window Stencil from Etsy.

Another effective way to help birds see house windows as a barrier is to stick on clear collision tape like CollidEscape, available from Amazon. To be effective against bird strikes, and therefore cut down on curious birds pecking at what they perceive as an invisible wall, you’ll need to position the tape in vertical or horizontal stripes with the edges no more than 2 inches apart. If you have feathered friends that often peck at a particular part of a window, this is a useful method as you can reduce the gap between strips here.

If a particular bird still persists in pecking at a window, creating a temporary cardboard barrier can help break the habit.

If you have a problem with a particularly territorial or bigger bird such as a woodpecker or seagull, a final resort is to fix a permanent deterrent near to the targeted window. Wind-powered metal spinners throw out unpredictable flashes of light, visually confusing birds to create an area they perceive as unsafe. Windmill spinners like these Stainless Steel Bird Deterrent Devices by Ebern Designs on Wayfair mean you don’t have to compromise on garden style.

Backyard birds need our support more than ever once fall turns to winter, whether that's preventing a bird bath freezing over to preserve their water supply, saving up kitchen scraps to feed feathered friends, or making sure smaller songbirds get a fair share of food. Now you understand why birds tap on windows in fall, you can decide whether or not to ignore the behaviour or take action for your and the bird's benefit.
